newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Angry Prodi rejects talk of Italian EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Angry Prodi rejects talk of Italian EMU delay.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi rejected a report on Wednesday that Italy would be offered delayed entry to Europe's planned currency union and said the country was "solemnly committed" to meeting membership terms from the start.

"The Italian government...deplores the constant repetition of false stories and unjustified statements, including from authoritative media, which have no foundation whatsoever," a statement from Prodi's office said.
"They do nothing but generate uncertainty among Italians and on financial markets," it said.
Prodi, appointed last May, has pegged his survival to ensuring Italy's debt-burdened economy is in shape to join Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from its January 1999 start.
He issued his statement after a Financial Times report that senior European central bankers and monetary officials were working on a plan to allow Italy in from 2000 or 2001.

The report called the purported plan a "face saving compromise" to assuage German fears that initial Italian entry would weaken the planned single currency, the euro, and said it could be extended to other countries such as Spain and Portugal.

"Prime Minister Romano Prodi...reaffirms Italy's firm intention and solemn commitment to meet the convergence criteria envisaged under the Maastricht Treaty within the time foreseen," Wednesday's statement said.
Insistent speculation of an Italian EMU delay has grown louder in the run-up to talks in Bonn on Friday between Prodi and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

While Prodi has voiced confidence that Italy will make the grade, several senior German bankers have openly expressed fears that the sort of budgetary rigour Italy is adopting this year is not sustainable.

"Every time the prospect of Italy entering EMU becomes more concrete, people in some financial circles get a belly ache," a senior Italian Treasury official said. "We're going to see a lot of reports like this between now and the first half of 1998."
European Union leaders will meet early next year to decide which countries should be in EMU from the outset. Prodi has said he would resign if Italy is not among them.

Prodi has inflicted unpopular budgetary medicine on voters, including 1997 tax hikes, to try to ensure that Italy's deficit this year stays within three per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), one of the fundamental EMU yardsticks.
Germany and France both said on Wednesday that they were not engaged in any talks on a compromise entry for Italy.
Despite the denials, European Union officials said a compromise plan delaying Italy's membership into the next century was under consideration by certain governments.
"I can't confirm to which extent this is something which has been completely worked out, but in some quarters people are definitely thinking about this," a senior EU official said.
Economic commentators say any hint at this stage that Rome may join EMU late would undermine Prodi's effort to clean up public finances.
The speculation has also given the opposition a stick with which to beat the centre-left government, which it accuses of pursuing mistaken economic policies that will not get Italy in to EMU.
